defects: Image does not support a sufficiently distinct teaching answer: The branching tubular lucent pattern overlying the right hepatic lobe is visible and extends peripherally toward the liver edge, which is the key imaging feature being tested. However, the independent read correctly notes that on plain film alone, peripheral biliary gas (pneumobilia) and portal venous gas cannot be reliably distinguished — both produce branching hepatic lucencies. Portal venous gas classically distributes peripherally (as seen here), while pneumobilia tends toward central ducts, but this distinction is not reliable on supine AP radiograph without CT. The stomach gas bubble is visible in the left upper quadrant. The lumbar spine is visible centrally. Colonic gas is distributed throughout. The abdomen extends well below the umbilicus into the pelvis and lower abdomen, which exceeds the expected crop at the navel. No duplication, impossible anatomy, or AI artifact is identified in the non-pathological structures.

findings: Anteroposterior (AP) supine abdominal radiograph including the lower thorax
Extensive branching, tree-like radiolucent pattern overlying the right hepatic lobe consistent with pneumobilia or intrahepatic biliary gas extending to the periphery of the liver
No discrete pneumoperitoneum identified on this supine projection
Stomach fundus visible in the left upper quadrant with a gas-filled bubble
Lumbar spine visible centrally with mild dextroscoliosis or rotational positioning artifact
Scattered colonic gas throughout the large bowel; no definitive dilated small bowel loops identified
Lower thorax partially included; no obvious pleural effusion or consolidation on this limited view
No calcified gallstones or renal calculi identified
Soft tissue density appears preserved bilaterally in the flanks
differential: Pneumobilia secondary to biliary-enteric anastomosis or prior sphincterotomy/ERCP (most common benign cause of peripheral intrahepatic gas)
Pneumobilia secondary to emphysematous cholecystitis or ascending cholangitis with gas-forming organisms
Hepatic portal venous gas (though distribution appears more central/biliary in branching pattern; portal venous gas typically more peripheral — cannot fully exclude on plain film alone)
anatomyConcerns: The branching gas pattern extends to the liver periphery, which favors biliary rather than portal venous distribution, but definitive distinction requires CT
Supine projection limits detection of free intraperitoneal air; erect or left lateral decubitus view would be recommended if pneumoperitoneum is a clinical concern
Lower chest is partially included but lung bases are not fully assessed
